frozen_original.title: BLM Opens 250,000 Wyoming Acres Near Yellowstone and Grand Teton to Oil Drilling
frozen_original.synopsis: Interior Secretary Doug Burgum signed a secretarial order in February 2025 requiring BLM to prioritize reducing barriers to energy development on public lands and shorten permitting timelines from two years to 28 days under emergency procedures. The administration's 2025 Wyoming lease sales offered 45,804 acres near Yellowstone for oil and gas drilling, followed by a proposed 2026 auction of over 250,000 Wyoming acres, including more than 88,000 acres overlapping all three state-designated mule deer migration corridors and the pronghorn corridor adjacent to Grand Teton National Park. The Big Beautiful Bill additionally mandated that at least 50% of all industry-nominated public lands be made available for leasing, removing BLM's conservation-based discretion.

primary.split_rationale: The frozen record combines a February 2025 Interior policy-order event with a separate June 2026 Wyoming lease sale. The two events are independently described by accessed government sources and have distinct dates; the unsupported 250,000-acre and migration-corridor claims are omitted.

children.title: Interior Orders Review to Unleash American Energy
children.description_short: Interior Orders Review to Unleash American Energy
children.description_medium: On February 3, 2025, Interior Secretary Doug Burgum announced six new Secretary’s Orders, including Order 3418. The Department said it would encourage energy production on federal lands and review agency actions that could burden domestic energy development. The documented action is a policy direction; the sources do not establish resulting drilling or environmental effects.
children.description_long: On February 3, 2025, Interior Secretary Doug Burgum announced that he had signed six Secretary’s Orders on his first day in office. The Department described Secretary’s Order 3418, “Unleashing American Energy,” as aligning Interior with the president’s energy policy, encouraging energy exploration and production on federal lands and waters, and requiring review of agency actions that could burden domestic energy-resource development. The order also directed review of certain appropriations. This card records the policy direction and review instructions, not a measured change in drilling, leasing outcomes, or environmental conditions. The original entry’s Wyoming acreage and migration-corridor claims concern later lease events and are separated into another child. No 28-day permitting guarantee, acreage figure, or migration-corridor effect is carried into this copy because the accessed evidence for the February order does not establish those claims. The record identifies a federal policy direction with nationwide reach across Interior; operational effects and environmental outcomes remain unknown.

children.title: BLM Leases 114,439 Acres in June 2026 Wyoming Oil and Gas Sale
children.description_short: BLM Leases 114,439 Acres in June 2026 Wyoming Oil and Gas Sale
children.description_medium: On June 9, 2026, BLM reported leasing 102 Wyoming parcels totaling about 114,439 acres for $34.7 million in receipts. Its earlier notice had proposed 108 parcels and 119,595 acres. The sources establish a completed lease sale, not actual drilling or wildlife effects; leasing is only the first step before separate permit review.
children.description_long: On June 9, 2026, the Bureau of Land Management reported that it leased 102 Wyoming parcels totaling approximately 114,439 acres in a quarterly oil and gas sale, with $34,706,638 in total receipts. In March, the agency had announced 108 parcels totaling 119,595 acres for a planned June sale, so the final sale did not match the earlier offered-parcel total in the held entry. BLM states that leasing is the first step in federal oil and gas development and that an operator must submit an application for a permit to drill before development can begin. The supplied claim that the sale covered 250,000 acres near Yellowstone and Grand Teton or overlapped named wildlife migration corridors is not supported by the accessed sale notices and is omitted. These sources document leases and receipts, not actual drilling, production, emissions, or specific wildlife effects. The receipt total is reported by BLM and is not treated here as long-term government revenue or private profit. The event is a completed lease sale; later development and environmental outcomes remain unknown.

source_fact_map.fact: BLM announced a planned June 2026 sale of 108 parcels totaling 119,595 Wyoming acres.
source_fact_map.quote: to offer 108 oil and gas parcels totaling 119,595 acres in Wyoming.
source_fact_map.source_excerpt: The Bureau of Land Management today announced an oil and gas lease sale scheduled for June 2, 2026, to offer 108 oil and gas parcels totaling 119,595 acres in Wyoming. The BLM completed scoping on these parcels in November 2025 and held a public comment period that closed in January 2026 on the parcels and the related environmental analysis. A 30-day public protest period to receive additional public input opened today and will close April 20, 2026. Leasing is the first step in the process to develop federal oil and gas resources. Before development operations can begin, an operator must submit an application for permit to drill detailing development plans.

frozen_original.title: Iran Closes Strait of Hormuz — Oil Prices Spike 40%
frozen_original.synopsis: In June 2025, Iran temporarily closed the Strait of Hormuz — the narrow waterway through which approximately 20% of the world's traded oil passes — in response to US-Israeli strikes on its nuclear facilities. The closure lasted several days before US naval pressure and international diplomacy forced a partial reopening. During the closure, global oil prices spiked over 40%, triggering a stock market selloff, inflation concerns, and emergency meetings of the International Energy Agency. Countries dependent on Persian Gulf oil imports, including Japan, South Korea, and India, faced acute supply disruptions. The episode demonstrated the global economic vulnerability created by Trump's decision to pursue military solutions over diplomacy.

primary.title: Tankers Turn Away and Pause Near Hormuz After U.S. Strikes on Iran
primary.description_short: Tankers Turn Away and Pause Near Hormuz After U.S. Strikes on Iran
primary.description_medium: On June 23, 2025, Reuters reported that at least two supertankers turned away near the Strait of Hormuz after U.S. strikes on Iran, while other ships paused or altered routes amid fears of a possible Iranian closure. Iran’s parliament had approved a closure measure, but it still required Supreme National Security Council approval; Reuters said Iran had never closed the strait. The report documents precautionary diversions, not a multi-day closure or a 40% oil-price spike.
primary.description_long: Reuters reporting dated June 23, 2025, described changes in tanker routes after U.S. military strikes on Iran. Ship-tracking data showed at least two supertankers made U-turns near the Strait of Hormuz; several other vessels altered course or anchored outside the route. The report said the U.S. decision to join Israel’s attacks had increased fears of retaliation that might close the strait, through which about 20% of global oil and gas demand flows. It noted Iran’s parliament had approved a measure to close the waterway, but that it still required approval from the Supreme National Security Council; Reuters added that Iran had threatened closure before but never done so. The verified event is heightened shipping risk and precautionary vessel diversions. The available report does not substantiate a multi-day Iranian closure or the frozen record’s claim that global oil prices spiked more than 40% because of one. It also reports no completed closure or measured supply interruption.

frozen_original.title: Bondi DOJ Investigates Manhattan DA Alvin Bragg for Trump Hush Money Prosecution
frozen_original.synopsis: In February 2025, the Trump DOJ opened an investigation into Manhattan District Attorney Alvin Bragg — who had prosecuted Trump in the hush money criminal case resulting in 34 felony convictions — examining whether Bragg's office had improperly coordinated with federal authorities or misused state resources, in what Bragg's team and legal scholars universally described as a pretextual federal investigation designed to punish him for the Trump prosecution. The investigation represented a federal incursion into state prosecutorial independence with no historical parallel, weaponizing federal investigative resources to retaliate against a local prosecutor for exercising lawful state jurisdiction. Bragg's office cooperated with the investigation while condemning its political motivation. The episode was part of a coordinated campaign against all prosecutors who had pursued criminal charges against Trump, establishing the precedent that prosecuting a former president invited federal retaliation.

primary.title: Bondi DOJ Working Group Ordered Review of Federal Actions Involving Alvin Bragg
primary.description_short: A February 2025 DOJ memo directed a working-group review that included alleged federal cooperation with Alvin Bragg’s Trump prosecution.
primary.description_medium: On February 5, 2025, Attorney General Pam Bondi created the DOJ Weaponization Working Group and directed it to review federal enforcement activity from the previous four years. The memo included alleged federal cooperation with Manhattan District Attorney Alvin Bragg’s Trump prosecution among the subjects for review. It did not establish that allegation, announce a Bragg-specific criminal investigation, or find that Bragg acted improperly.
primary.description_long: On February 5, 2025, Attorney General Pam Bondi issued a memo establishing the Justice Department’s Weaponization Working Group. The directive assigned the group a review of federal civil and criminal enforcement activities during the previous four years and called for quarterly progress reports to the White House. Its list of topics included what the memo called “federal cooperation with the weaponization” by Manhattan District Attorney Alvin Bragg, New York Attorney General Letitia James, their staffs, and other New York officials against Donald Trump and his businesses. That language states the administration’s allegation and the subject of a review; it is not a finding that Bragg coordinated with federal authorities or acted unlawfully. The memo also does not announce a criminal investigation into Bragg. The frozen entry’s claim that DOJ opened a February investigation into Bragg, along with its assertions about Bragg’s cooperation and a coordinated campaign against prosecutors, is not supported by the material reviewed and is omitted. The documented event is the DOJ review directive concerning the earlier Trump prosecutions.
